title: Managing product delivery: team planning and team retrospective
blurb: Explain the four managing product delivery activities and the topics of the team planning and team retrospective workshops.
question: A delivery team refines its backlog, estimates stories and selects work for the next iteration, then later reflects on what went well and what to improve. Which process and workshops are these?

teach.body: Managing product delivery controls the link between the project manager and the delivery team, by agreeing how work is accepted, executed, reported and delivered. It is the delivering level: the product owner, a version of the team manager, works with a self-managing delivery team. Work arrives as a set of user stories, and detailed task-level planning is done here, for the next iteration.

steps.sub: tell the PM it is done

teach.body: To accept a work package, the delivery team reviews the set of user stories, produces a team plan showing what can be completed within the constraints, reviews risks, advises the PM and agrees to deliver. Executing means doing the work, telling the PM about completed quality activities and getting approvals. Evaluating means reviewing registers and logs and updating the team dashboard so the PM can pull information. Finally the team notifies the PM that the package is complete.

Its purpose is to prepare the team for the coming iteration: refine the product backlog, clarify requirements, prioritize user stories and agree the team plan. Participants set clear acceptance criteria, estimate effort together and build a focused iteration plan that fits the project objectives.

Goal
rows: Clarify and prioritize (MoSCoW); align with objectives
Clear, testable acceptance criteria; agree what 'done' means
Shared view of each story's complexity and effort
Select stories; a realistic team plan for the iteration

teach.body: At the end of each iteration the team reflects on it: celebrating successes, identifying challenges and capturing lessons to drive continual improvement. Risks are also gathered here, as in every planning session and retrospective. Retrospectives look back over the finished iteration; they are not a tool for tracking progress during it.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mercia Fire and Rescue
teach.body: Product owner Hannah Lee's team is building a station inspection app for Mercia Fire and Rescue. In team planning they rank stories with MoSCoW, tighten acceptance criteria, estimate with story points and pick what fits the iteration, producing their team plan. At the retrospective, run by team coach Tomasz Nowak, they celebrate a smooth offline mode, discuss a late design hand-off, agree to pair on complex stories next time, and finish with a quiz.

teach.text: The DELIVERY TEAM produces the team plan when accepting a work package; the CPO prioritizes the project backlog, not the team's plan. Improvement suggestions go under 'the learning', not 'the bad'. And task-level planning happens in team planning, not in release planning at a stage boundary.

items: Managing product delivery: the link between PM and delivery team.
Activities: accept, execute, evaluate, notify work package completion.
Team plan produced by the delivery team when accepting the work package.
Team planning: backlog refinement, story refinement, effort estimation, iteration planning.
Team retrospective: the good, the bad, the learning, team building.
Detailed planning for the next iteration only.

summary: You can now describe the four managing product delivery activities and the topics of the team planning and team retrospective workshops. You can also tell team planning apart from release planning.

A.q: When a work package is accepted, who produces the team plan showing what can be completed within the constraints?
A.why: The delivery team reviews the set of user stories and produces a team plan (Table 13.12).

whyNot.0: The PM authorizes the work package and reviews the team plan.
whyNot.2: The CPO owns and prioritizes the project backlog.
whyNot.3: The team coach facilitates and supports self-management.

A.q: Which managing product delivery activity tells the project manager that the work package is complete?
A.why: Notify work package completion is where the team informs the PM (Table 13.12).

whyNot.0: Accepting covers reviewing the stories and producing the team plan.
whyNot.1: Executing covers the work, quality activities and approvals.
whyNot.2: Evaluating covers registers, logs and the team dashboard.

A.q: Which team planning topic gives a shared understanding of the complexity and effort of each prioritized story?
A.why: Effort estimation builds a shared view of each story's complexity and effort (Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: Backlog refinement clarifies and prioritizes requirements.
whyNot.1: Story refinement makes acceptance criteria clear and testable.
whyNot.3: Iteration planning selects stories using the estimates.

B.q: What is the purpose of the team retrospective workshop?
options: To reflect on the last iteration and drive improvement
To demonstrate completed features to the users
To refine and estimate the product backlog
To review agile adoption risks with the board
B.why: The team retrospective reflects on the latest iteration, celebrating successes, identifying challenges and capturing lessons (13.6.4.2).

whyNot.1: Demonstrating features is the product demo in the progress review.
whyNot.2: Refining and estimating is team planning.
whyNot.3: Agile adoption risks are reviewed in the agile enablement workshop.

B.q: Which team planning topic checks that the acceptance criteria of high-priority stories are clear and testable?
B.why: User story refinement aligns on what counts as done for each story and sets a clear testing path (Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: Backlog refinement prioritizes requirements with MoSCoW.
whyNot.1: Iteration planning selects stories for the iteration.

B.q: In which activity does the team review registers and logs and update the team dashboard so the PM can pull current information?
B.why: Evaluate a work package includes reviewing registers and logs and updating the team dashboard (Table 13.12).

whyNot.1: Executing delivers the work and obtains approvals.
whyNot.2: Notifying tells the PM that the work package is complete.

C.q: In a team retrospective, a developer suggests pairing on complex stories next iteration. Which topic is this, and in which process does the workshop sit?
options: The learning; managing a stage boundary
C.why: Improvement suggestions belong under the learning, and the team retrospective supports managing product delivery (Table 13.14).

whyNot.0: The bad names problems and causes; the workshop is not in controlling a stage.
whyNot.2: Team building strengthens bonds; it does not hold improvement actions.
whyNot.3: The topic is right, but the workshop belongs to managing product delivery.

C.q:
Which two statements about managing product delivery are correct?
1. Iteration planning selects stories for the next iteration using priorities and estimates.
2. The team retrospective includes a product demo for users.
3. When executing a work package, the team obtains approvals for completed products.
4. The release map for the next stage is updated in this process.
C.why: Iteration planning selects stories by priority and estimate (Table 13.13), and executing includes obtaining approvals (Table 13.12).

whyNot.1: Statement 2 is wrong: the product demo is in the progress review workshop.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: the demo is in the progress review, and the next stage's release map is updated at a stage boundary.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the next stage's release map is a stage boundary output.

C.q: Detailed task-level planning for the next iteration happens in which workshop, supporting which process?
options: Release planning workshop; managing a stage boundary
Project initiation workshop; initiating a project
Team planning workshop; managing product delivery
Progress review workshop; controlling a stage
C.why: The team planning workshop in managing product delivery produces the team plan for the next iteration (13.6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Release planning updates the release map for the next stage at a higher level.
whyNot.1: The project initiation workshop produces the high-level release map.
whyNot.3: The progress review assesses status and demos the product.

reteach.title: A band rehearsing for a gig
reteach.question: How does a band's week map onto managing product delivery?

blocks.body: The promoter asks for a 40-minute set (the work package). The band picks songs, agrees how polished each must be and guesses how long each takes to learn: team planning. They rehearse, tell the promoter when ready and, after the gig, talk about what worked, what went wrong, what to change, then go for a curry: the team retrospective.

blocks.text: The band writes its own set list; the promoter (PM) does not plan the band's rehearsals.

explain.body: Managing product delivery controls the link between the PM and the delivery team through agreed requirements for acceptance, execution, reporting and delivery.

test.q: What is the purpose of managing product delivery?
options: To assign work and keep the stage within tolerance
To let the board make key decisions and keep control
To lay solid foundations before significant spend
To control the link between the PM and the delivery team
test.why: That is the purpose of managing product delivery (13.6.1).

explain.body: While executing a work package, the team does the work, notifies the PM of completed quality activities and products, and obtains approvals for completed products.

test.q: What does the team do when executing a work package?
options: Delivers the work, reports quality activities and gets approvals
Reviews the stories and produces a team plan within constraints
Reviews registers and logs and updates the team dashboard
Informs the project manager that the package is complete
test.why: Executing covers the work, reporting completed quality activities and obtaining approvals (Table 13.12).

whyNot.1: That is accepting a work package.
whyNot.2: That is evaluating a work package.
whyNot.3: That is notifying work package completion.

explain.body: Backlog refinement prioritizes with MoSCoW; story refinement sharpens acceptance criteria; effort estimation sizes stories; iteration planning builds the team plan.

test.q: Which team planning topic prioritizes requirements with MoSCoW so the product backlog aligns with project objectives?
test.why: Product backlog refinement clarifies requirements and prioritizes them with MoSCoW (Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: Story refinement focuses on acceptance criteria.
whyNot.2: Iteration planning selects stories for the iteration.

explain.body: The good celebrates wins; the bad names issues, risks, challenges and their causes; the learning sets improvement actions; team building strengthens bonds.

test.q: Which team retrospective topic identifies issues, risks and challenges and their causes?
test.why: The bad pinpoints areas for growth by discussing issues, risks and challenges and their causes (Table 13.14).

whyNot.1: The learning turns lessons into actions.
